original_value: AbstractWe present a novel approach to optimally retarget videos for varied displays with differing aspect ratios by preserving salient scene content discovered via eye tracking. Our algorithm performs editing with cut, pan and zoom operations by optimizing the path of a cropping window within the original video while seeking to (i) preserve salient regions, and (ii) adhere to the principles of cinematography. Our approach is (a) content agnostic as the same methodology is employed to re‐edit a wide‐angle video recording or a close‐up movie sequence captured with a static or moving camera, and (b) independent of video length and can in principle re‐edit an entire movie in one shot.Our algorithm consists of two steps. The first step employs gaze transition cues to detect time stamps where new cuts are to be introduced in the original video via dynamic programming. A subsequent step optimizes the cropping window path (to create pan and zoom effects), while accounting for the original and new cuts. The cropping window path is designed to include maximum gaze information, and is composed of piecewise constant, linear and parabolic segments. It is obtained via L(1)regularized convex optimization which ensures a smooth viewing experience. We test our approach on a wide variety of videos and demonstrate significant improvement over the state‐of‐the‐art, both in terms of computational complexity and qualitative aspects. A study performed with 16 users confirms that our approach results in a superior viewing experience as compared to gaze driven re‐editing [JSSH15] and letterboxing methods, especially for wide‐angle static camera recordings.

result.paraphrase: Abstract We propose a novel method for optimally retargeting videos to displays with different aspect ratios by preserving salient scene content identified through eye tracking. The algorithm edits footage using cut, pan, and zoom operations by optimizing the trajectory of a cropping window within the original video while aiming to (i) retain salient regions and (ii) follow cinematographic principles. It is both (a) content agnostic, since the same method can re-edit either a wide-angle recording or a close-up movie sequence captured with a static or moving camera, and (b) independent of video length, so in principle an entire movie can be re-edited in one pass. The algorithm has two stages. First, gaze transition cues are used with dynamic programming to detect timestamps where new cuts should be introduced in the original video. Next, the cropping-window path is optimized to create pan and zoom effects while respecting both the original and newly inserted cuts. The path is constructed to capture the maximum amount of gaze information and consists of piecewise constant, linear, and parabolic segments. It is derived through L(1)-regularized convex optimization, ensuring a smooth viewing experience. Experiments on a broad range of videos show substantial gains over the state of the art in both computational complexity and qualitative results. A study with 16 users confirms that the method provides a better viewing experience than gaze-driven re-editing [JSSH15] and letterboxing, especially for wide-angle static-camera recordings.
